item.title: The cost of simulating classically tractable quantum circuits and dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Polynomial-time classical simulations of quantum dynamics are often outpaced by direct quantum hardware execution due to high one-time quantum sampling and shadow post-processing overheads when preparing unknown input states.

Grade 0.409 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation” · Su Yeon Chang, Supanut Thanasilp, Zoë Holmes, M. Cerezo

Figure

Estimated total wall-clock time versus qubit count n for direct quantum simulation and classical simulation across IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron architectures.

Asks

Whether classically simulable quantum evolutions are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically or to execute directly on quantum hardware.

But

Independent unentangled input copies only (no multi-copy quantum memory); unitaries and observables restricted to efficient classical representations.

Tools

classical shadows · Lie-algebraic simulation (g-sim) · Pauli Propagation · Majorana Propagation · hardware pricing models

Abstract

Determining whether a quantum evolution can be efficiently simulated classically is central to understanding the boundary between classical and quantum computation. However, polynomial-time simulability is an asymptotic statement, and does not by itself determine whether the (quantum-inspired) classical simulation is actually practical. Indeed, different polynomial scalings can lead to vastly different computational costs, particularly when expensive preprocessing or quantum data acquisition is required. In this work, we ask whether classically simulable quantum dynamics are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically than to execute directly on quantum hardware. We analyze this question using three resource metrics, quantum sample, quantum time, and classical time complexity, for several widely studied classically simulable circuit families. Using representative hardware-level estimates, we identify regimes in which quantum simulation can be faster despite the existence of a polynomial-time classical algorithm, as well as regimes in which classical simulation remains more efficient. At the same time, the large quantum sampling cost needed to characterize unknown input states can make this polynomial-time classical simulation prohibitively expensive with current cloud-based hardware access prices. Ultimately, our work indicates that guarantees of classical simulability with polynomial resources alone are insufficient to determine the preferred implementation.

item.title: One-clean-qubit spectroscopy of simulated Kitaev chains
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Extracts full 2N eigenenergies of an N-site transverse-field Ising model and the N single-particle energies of its mapped Kitaev chain via stroboscopic DQC1 readout on a single control spin.

Grade 0.385 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Z. M. McIntyre, Daniel Loss

Figure

Stroboscopic control-qubit expectation value vs time, showing resolution of single-particle Kitaev spectrum across trivial and topological regimes under 1/f noise.

Asks

How can the full spectrum and topological crossover of a simulated Kitaev chain be extracted in quantum-dot spin qubit arrays lacking multi-qubit simultaneous readout?

But

Requires simulation time Ttot>2π/δϵmin⁡ and gate infidelity εgate<min⁡[1/(N(J+h)Ttot),δϵmin⁡2/(Nh2)]; demonstrated numerically for N=6.

Tools

Digital-analog quantum simulation · One-clean-qubit (DQC1) model · Jordan-Wigner transformation · Repetition-code control qubit · Drive-engineered Floquet Hamiltonian

Abstract

Spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots provide a highly programmable platform for simulating condensed-matter phenomena. In this work, we introduce a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol for extracting the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain. The Kitaev chain is mapped onto qubits via the standard Jordan-Wigner transformation and implemented as a drive-engineered, N-site transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in a linear array of quantum dots. We show that periodically toggling the analog-simulation parameters conditioned on the state of a control qubit causes the dynamics of this control qubit to stroboscopically match the output of the one-clean-qubit (DQC1) model of computation, thereby yielding the full spectrum of the TFIM from measurements of a single spin. Classical postprocessing can then be used to isolate the N single-particle energies of the Kitaev chain from the 2^N eigenenergies of the TFIM. By varying the strength of the Rabi drive used to engineer the synthetic transverse field, the spectral signature of the crossover from the trivial to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain could then be mapped out with measurements of just one spin.

item.title: Joint Mitigation of Algorithmic and Physical Errors in Noisy Hamiltonian Simulation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Tying physical-noise strength to Trotter step size as λ(s)=c(sT)p+1 aligns physical and algorithmic errors at order sp, letting a single 1D Richardson extrapolation replace 2D grid extrapolation with provable commutator-scaling resource overhead.

Grade 0.343 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Shuo Zhou, Xinzhao Wang, Ruiqi Zhang, Xiaoyang Wang, Yi-Cong Zheng, Tongang Li, Shengyu Zhang

Figure

Comparison of error-mitigation paths on the step size s vs noise strength λ plane: 2D rectangular Richardson grid needing independent zero-noise and Trotter extrapolations versus coupled 1D path λ(s)=c(sT)p+1 reaching (0,0) in a single fit.

Asks

Can joint extrapolation along a single coupled path simultaneously eliminate algorithmic Trotter bias and hardware noise while preserving provable commutator scaling?

Before

Sequential/2D extrapolation requiring an m×m′ grid of circuit evaluations with independent Trotter and zero-noise fits.

But

Requires noise strengths above the intrinsic device-noise floor; assumes local Hamiltonians with local Lindbladian noise.

Tools

finite-order Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff truncation · Richardson extrapolation · learned sparse Pauli-Lindblad noise amplification · Sparse Pauli Dynamics

Abstract

Product-formula Hamiltonian simulation is naturally suited to near-term quantum processors, but its accuracy is set by two competing errors: finite-step Trotter bias and physical hardware noise. We introduce a joint extrapolation strategy that ties the tunable per-layer noise strength to the Trotter step size, λ(s)=c(sT)^(p+1) for a p-th order product formula. Along this one-dimensional path, the leading physical-noise and Trotter corrections over the full evolution both enter at order s^p and can be canceled by a single Richardson extrapolation. Building on a previously established finite-order Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff truncation bound, we derive a provably commutator-scaling resource guarantee for the joint extrapolation. For local Hamiltonians with local Lindbladian noise, the protocol mitigates physical noise together with Trotter error with only a constant asymptotic overhead relative to noiseless Trotter extrapolation, provided the required noise strengths lie above the intrinsic device-noise floor. We experimentally demonstrate the protocol for Ising dynamics on a superconducting quantum computer using learned noise amplification. Complementary 100-qubit Sparse Pauli Dynamics (SPD) simulations achieve comparable accuracy to two-dimensional Richardson extrapolation with fewer circuit settings.

item.title: Distributed variational quantum computing with deterministic entanglement tuning
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Distributed variational quantum computing protocol deterministically tunes shared Bell-pair entanglement via LOCC with unit success probability (pM=1) and concurrence 𝒞M(θ)=cos⁡θ, keeping state infidelity below 0.05 across full range.

Grade 0.340 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation” · Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim

Figure

Concurrence (top) and state infidelity (bottom) plotted against the tuning angle θ, demonstrating deterministic modulation of entanglement from 1 down to 0 while keeping state infidelity below 0.05.

Asks

How can entanglement between distributed quantum processing units be tuned continuously and deterministically without the probabilistic losses of filtering or the high Bell-pair consumption of gate teleportation?

But

Demonstrated on bipartite single-qubit photonic processors; feed-forward conditional operations performed offline rather than in real time; pure-state majorization requires initial entanglement to be equal to or greater than target.

Tools

spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) · displaced Sagnac interferometer · POVM with path-mode ancilla · COBYLA optimization · quantum state tomography

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H⁺ molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.

item.title: Quantum transport along a tight-binding chain connected to Markovian reservoirs
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Stationary current across a tight-binding chain coupled to boundary Markovian reservoirs is derived analytically for arbitrary on-site dephasing κ. At κ=0, inter-site currents follow an asymmetric Laplace distribution with covariance cov(ℐˆℓ,ℐˆℓ+1)=Ist2/2 and zero covariance for separation |ℓ−ℓ′|≥2.

Grade 0.338 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · P. S. Muraev, A. R. Kolovsky, D. N. Maksimov

Figure

Probability distribution of bond and boundary currents plotted against analytical predictions (red curves) from stochastic simulations (bins) for κ=0.

Asks

What are the exact stationary current, site populations, and current fluctuation distributions in a boundary-driven tight-binding chain with dephasing?

But

Non-interacting particles (bosons or fermions). Full many-body characteristic function and current distributions derived specifically for bosons in the absence of dephasing (κ=0).

Tools

Lindblad master equation · Single-particle density matrix (SPDM) · Phase-space / characteristic function formalism · Itô stochastic drift-diffusion simulations

Abstract

We consider quantum transport of non-interacting particles in a tight-binding chain coupled to Markovian reservoirs at its boundaries and subject to uniform on-site dephasing. Using the masterequation approach, we derived the exact analytic solution for the mean current along the chain. This analytic solution is obtained in the framework of single-particle quantum mechanics and, thus, equally applies for transport of non-interacting bosons and fermions. In the absence of phase damping, the results are extended to the complete many-body solution for bosonic problem in the form of anti-normally ordered characteristic function. This function allows us to calculate the distribution function for the current at each bond in the chain as well as the inter-bond current correlation functions.

item.title: Instabilities in self-consistent diagrammatic approaches and how to cure them
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Misleading convergence in self-consistent boson-exchange schemes (TRILEX, SBE, MBE) is caused solely by algorithmic iteration instability—where Jacobian eigenvalues exceed unity—rather than fundamental multivaluedness of the Luttinger–Ward functional. Inverting the unstable Jacobian eigendirections stabilizes convergence to exact physical solutions across strong-coupling regimes and through vertex divergences.

Grade 0.336 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Marcel Gievers, Herbert Eßl, Stefan Rohshap, Anna Kauch, Alessandro Toschi

Figure

Phase space of coupling βU versus chemical potential shift βδμ. Shaded regions mark where standard iteration fails (|jα|>1), defining the threshold mixing parameter p(c=1) required for stability across TRILEX, SBE, and MBE.

Asks

What causes self-consistent diagrammatic boson-exchange algorithms to converge to unphysical fixed points at intermediate-to-strong electronic coupling, and how can they be stabilized?

But

Demonstrated on exactly solvable local models (Hubbard atom and zero-point model) without spatial momentum dependence.

Tools

Boson-exchange formalism (TRILEX, SBE, MBE) · Jacobian eigenspectrum inversion · Hubbard atom model · Zero-point model

Abstract

While self-consistent diagrammatic approaches are widely used to compute the physical properties of correlated quantum materials, their applicability may get severely hindered precisely in the parameter regions, where the most exciting physics is observed. One of the major issues, referred to as "misleading convergence", is the tendency of iterative schemes to converge to unphysical fixed points for intermediate-to-strong electronic interactions, regardless of numerical accuracy of the computation. Here, we explicitly verify that the origin of this problem in several established self-consistent many-electron approaches, defined in the general diagrammatic framework of the boson-exchange formalism, resides exclusively in the stability condition of the respective iteration schemes, and not in an intrinsic breakdown of their self-consistent diagrammatic description. This insight enables a simple and general remedy, as recently proposed in Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016502 (2026): The redefinition of the iterative procedure, by inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian associated to the fixed point of the self-consistent algorithm. We illustrate the successful outcome of this procedure by means of systematic calculations performed on testbed, exactly solvable, models. Our results demonstrate that the physical fixed point of the diagrammatic schemes we considered can be stabilized, de facto, across the entire parameter range, including the most challenging nonperturbative/strong-coupling regimes.

item.title: Local decoders for fault-tolerant quantum computation and translation-invariant stabilizer codes
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise with a non-zero threshold, and a 2D fault-tolerant quantum computer can operate using strictly local operations and constant quantum and classical resource density.

Grade 0.335 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Nathaniel Selub, Aditya Bhardwaj, Ethan Lake

Figure

Schematic of the 2D local fault-tolerant quantum architecture, showing a 1D array of folded surface-code patches decoded on-chip by constant-density classical cellular automata alongside a local 2D classical program-control computer.

Asks

Can scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation based on topological codes in fewer than four dimensions be implemented using strictly local operations, bounded communication speeds, and constant resource density?

Before

All prior local decoders for two-dimensional topological codes required per-site classical resources scaling at least polylogarithmically with system size, and prior fault-tolerant architectures in <4 spatial dimensions required non-local classical computation or communication.

But

Classical computation and communication components are assumed to be noiseless; phenomenological noise assumes p-bounded Pauli and bit-flip errors on data qubits and syndrome measurements.

Tools

cellular-automaton (CA) decoder · spacetime multiscale clustering · folded surface code · lattice surgery · hierarchical slice architecture

Abstract

We construct the first fully spatially local fault-tolerant quantum computer based on topological codes in fewer than four spatial dimensions. Our construction is a two-dimensional architecture that uses only geometrically local quantum and classical operations, bounded-speed classical communication and computation, and a constant density of quantum and classical resources. The core component is a new time-translation-invariant cellular-automaton decoder for the surface code. This decoder preserves logical information for a time stretched-exponential in the code distance and operates continuously during state injection, stabilizer-state preparation, lattice surgery, and transversal readout. We also prove that every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise.

item.arxave:question: Can scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation based on topological codes in fewer than four dimensions be implemented using strictly local operations, bounded communication speeds, and constant resource density?

item.arxave:abstract: We construct the first fully spatially local fault-tolerant quantum computer based on topological codes in fewer than four spatial dimensions. Our construction is a two-dimensional architecture that uses only geometrically local quantum and classical operations, bounded-speed classical communication and computation, and a constant density of quantum and classical resources. The core component is a new time-translation-invariant cellular-automaton decoder for the surface code. This decoder preserves logical information for a time stretched-exponential in the code distance and operates continuously during state injection, stabilizer-state preparation, lattice surgery, and transversal readout. We also prove that every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise.
